title: Databases for Automation (SQL Basics and Storing Data)
summary: As your automations grow, storing data in spreadsheets stops being enough, and knowing basic databases makes you far more capable and credible. Spreadsheets are great for small, simple data, but they slow down with volume, struggle with reliable look
content:
# Databases for Automation (SQL Basics and Storing Data) ##### The spreadsheet that hit the wall An events company built their entire registration system on Google Sheets. It worked beautifully for eighteen months — until a conference with 12,000 registrations. The symptoms arrived in order. First the sheet got slow to open. Then the automation started timing out because appending a row required loading the whole file. Then two staff members editing simultaneously created conflicting versions. Then someone sorted a range without selecting all columns and permanently scrambled the mapping between names and ticket numbers. Nobody could tell which row was corrupted, because there was no history and no constraint that would have prevented it. Every one of those failures has a name in database terms: **performance**, **concurrency**, **integrity**, **auditability**. Spreadsheets do not offer solutions to them because they were never designed to. Databases were — E.F. Codd's 1970 paper on the relational model set out exactly this problem and its solution. Today you learn enough SQL and enough database thinking to know when to graduate, and how. ##### When a spreadsheet is not enough Sheets remain a perfectly good choice for small, human-facing data. Move to a database when you hit any of these: - **Volume.** Beyond roughly 10,000–50,000 rows, spreadsheet operations get slow and API calls start timing out. Databases handle millions comfortably. - **Concurrency.** Multiple automations writing at once produce race conditions in a sheet. Databases handle simultaneous writes with transactions and locking. - **Data integrity.** A sheet cannot stop someone typing "forty-five" into a number column, or entering the same email twice. A database can — with types, `NOT NULL`, and `UNIQUE` constraints. - **Relationships.** Orders belonging to customers belonging to companies. Sheets fake this with lookup formulas; databases model it natively with foreign keys. - **Query complexity.** "Total revenue per city for customers who ordered more than twice last quarter" is one SQL statement and a nightmare of nested formulas. - **Auditability and security.** Row-level permissions, change logs, point-in-time backups. The honest counterweight: a spreadsheet is visible and editable by non-technical people, and that is a real feature. Many good systems use both — a database as the source of truth, with a synced sheet as the human-friendly view. ##### Relational databases and tables A **relational database** stores data in **tables**: rows (records) and columns (fields), where every column has a declared **type** and every table has a **primary key** uniquely identifying each row. Relationships come from **foreign keys** — a column in one table pointing at another table's primary key: ```text customers orders ───────────────────── ────────────────────────── id BIGSERIAL PK ◄──┐ id BIGSERIAL PK email TEXT UNIQUE └── customer_id BIGINT FK → customers.id full_name TEXT total_amount NUMERIC(12,2) city TEXT status TEXT created_at TIMESTAMPTZ created_at TIMESTAMPTZ ``` Creating that structure: ```sql CREATE TABLE customers ( id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE, full_name TEXT NOT NULL, city TEXT, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now() ); CREATE TABLE orders ( id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY, customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, total_amount NUMERIC(12,2) NOT NULL CHECK (total_amount >= 0), status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'new', created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now() ); CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer ON orders(customer_id); CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status ON orders(status); ``` Read what those constraints buy you. `UNIQUE` on email makes duplicate customers **structurally impossible** — the database rejects the insert, so the deduplication problem from CRM day is solved at the storage layer instead of in every workflow. `NOT NULL` guarantees required fields exist. `CHECK` prevents negative totals. `REFERENCES` guarantees no order points at a customer who does not exist. `NUMERIC(12,2)` stores money exactly, avoiding floating-point errors. Indexes make lookups on those columns fast. That is the deep difference: a spreadsheet *hopes* your data is clean; a database *enforces* it. ##### Basic SQL Four statements cover the vast majority of automation work. **SELECT** — read: ```sql -- everything SELECT * FROM customers; -- specific columns, filtered, sorted, limited SELECT full_name, email, city FROM customers WHERE city = 'Pune' AND created_at >= now() - interval '30 days' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50; -- joining two tables and aggregating SELECT c.full_name, c.email, COUNT(o.id) AS order_count, COALESCE(SUM(o.total_amount), 0) AS lifetime_value FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE c.city = 'Pune' GROUP BY c.id, c.full_name, c.email HAVING COUNT(o.id) > 2 ORDER BY lifetime_value DESC; ``` That second query — the one that would take a day of spreadsheet formulas — is the argument for SQL in twelve lines. **INSERT** — create: ```sql INSERT INTO customers (email, full_name, city) VALUES ('ananya@example.com', 'Ananya Rao', 'Pune') RETURNING id; ``` **UPDATE** — modify. Note the `WHERE`; without it you update every row in the table, which is a genuinely famous production disaster: ```sql UPDATE orders SET status = 'shipped', updated_at = now() WHERE id = 1042; ``` **DELETE** — remove, with the same warning: ```sql DELETE FROM orders WHERE status = 'cancelled' AND created_at < now() - interval '1 year'; ``` And the one advanced statement worth learning immediately, because it replaces the entire search-then-update-or-create pattern with a single atomic operation: ```sql INSERT INTO customers (email, full_name, city) VALUES ('ananya@example.com', 'Ananya Rao', 'Pune') ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE SET full_name = EXCLUDED.full_name, city = EXCLUDED.city, updated_at = now() RETURNING id, (xmax = 0) AS was_inserted; ``` This is an **upsert**. Because the database enforces uniqueness and handles the conflict atomically, there is no race condition between your lookup and your write — something a two-step workflow can never fully guarantee. ##### Connecting databases to your tools **n8n** ships with Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB and Supabase nodes. The Postgres node's Execute Query operation takes parameterized SQL: ```sql -- n8n Postgres node, with Query Parameters: {{ $json.email }}, {{ $json.name }} INSERT INTO customers (email, full_name) VALUES ($1, $2) ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE SET full_name = EXCLUDED.full_name RETURNING id; ``` Use `$1`, `$2` **parameters** rather than string-concatenating values into the query. Concatenation opens you to **SQL injection**, where a value like `'); DROP TABLE customers; --` becomes executable code. Parameterized queries send the value separately from the statement, so it can never be interpreted as SQL. **Make.com** has PostgreSQL and MySQL modules with the same capability. **Zapier** has more limited database support; a common pattern there is to call a small API you host, or use Airtable/Supabase's REST interface. From **Python**: ```python import os import psycopg2 from psycopg2.extras import RealDictCursor conn = psycopg2.connect(os.environ["DATABASE_URL"]) with conn, conn.cursor(cursor_factory=RealDictCursor) as cur: cur.execute( """ INSERT INTO customers (email, full_name, city) VALUES (%s, %s, %s) ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE SET full_name = EXCLUDED.full_name RETURNING id, email; """, ("ananya@example.com", "Ananya Rao", "Pune"), ) print(cur.fetchone()) cur.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM customers WHERE city = %s;", ("Pune",)) print(cur.fetchone()) ``` The `with conn` block wraps everything in a **transaction** — either all statements commit, or an exception rolls them all back. That all-or-nothing property is another thing spreadsheets simply cannot offer. ##### Hosted databases for beginners You do not need to run a server. Three good options: **Supabase** — managed PostgreSQL with a generous free tier, a browser-based table editor and SQL runner, an auto-generated REST API over your tables, authentication, and row-level security. It is the best learning choice because you get a *real* Postgres database with a friendly interface, and everything you learn transfers to any Postgres anywhere. **Airtable** — the friendliest, with typed fields, relations and a clean API, but it is a database-shaped product rather than SQL. Excellent when non-technical people need to browse and edit. **PlanetScale / Neon / Railway** — serverless MySQL and Postgres with free tiers, good when you want a plain connection string. Choosing between them: *Sheets* for tiny, human-edited data; *Airtable* for structured data non-technical users must manage; *Supabase/Postgres* when you need real integrity, volume, queries, or relationships. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Where should this data live?] --> B{Under ~1000 rows and
humans edit it directly?} B -->|yes| C[Google Sheets] B -->|no| D{Non-technical users need
to browse and edit?} D -->|yes| E[Airtable] D -->|no| F{Need constraints, joins,
volume, transactions?} F -->|yes| G[PostgreSQL / Supabase] F -->|no| E ``` ##### Common pitfalls - **`UPDATE` or `DELETE` without `WHERE`** — always write the `WHERE` clause first, then the rest. - **String-concatenated SQL** — SQL injection. Use parameters, always. - **No indexes** on columns you filter by — queries slow to a crawl as the table grows. - **Storing money as `FLOAT`** — use `NUMERIC`/`DECIMAL` or integer paise. - **Naive timestamps** — use `TIMESTAMPTZ` and store UTC. - **No primary key**, making individual rows unaddressable. - **Exposing the database directly to the internet** — use connection pooling, restrict IPs, and never put credentials in client-side code. - **Testing destructive queries on production.** Run `SELECT` with the same `WHERE` clause first to see exactly which rows you are about to change. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: set up a free **Supabase** project, create a table, and from an automation (n8n or Make) or a Python script **INSERT a record and then SELECT it back**. That round trip — write, then read to confirm — is the fundamental verification habit for database work, and it will catch mapping errors immediately. The mini project is the real graduation: **replace a spreadsheet backend with a database**. Create a table for leads or orders, update an existing automation to INSERT new records and UPDATE their status, and add a SELECT-based lookup to prevent duplicates. Better still, add a `UNIQUE` constraint and use `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` so duplicates become impossible rather than merely unlikely — then explain that improvement in your write-up. For the assignment, write the **four core SQL statements for a `customers` table** with realistic example values, and explain **three problems a database solves that a spreadsheet does not**. Pick from enforced integrity (unique emails, typed columns), safe concurrency (transactions, no race conditions), and query power with relationships (joins and aggregates in one statement). Concrete examples from your own mini project will make the answer land. ##### Key takeaways - Graduate from spreadsheets when you hit volume, concurrent writes, integrity needs, relationships, complex queries, or audit requirements. - Tables have typed columns, a primary key, and foreign keys; constraints like `UNIQUE`, `NOT NULL` and `CHECK` make bad data structurally impossible. - SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE cover most automation work — and `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` replaces the whole search-then-create pattern atomically. - Always parameterize queries to prevent SQL injection, and always write the `WHERE` clause before the rest of an UPDATE or DELETE. - Supabase gives you real managed PostgreSQL with a friendly UI and a free tier — the best place to learn skills that transfer everywhere.
